subtopic: INSPECTION OF CANADIAN PASSENGER BOATS
INSPECTION OF CANADIAN PASSENGER BOATS
speechtext:
1.	To what extent are Canadian boats which are licensed for passenger service, inspected before being put into service each season?
2.	IIow many inspectors are engaged by the government for this work, and to what extent do they inspect passenger service boats before allowing them to be put into service?
3.	Is it a fact that passenger boats plying in Canadian waters with a carrying capacity of one thousand passengers have only lifeboat equipment for less than two hundred people?

subtopic: INSPECTION OF CANADIAN PASSENGER BOATS
speechtext:
1.	(a) The boilers and machinery are opened out for inspection annually.
(b)	The hull as far as can be seen without the ship being taken out of the water is inspected annually, as is the lifesaving and other equipment.
(c)	Where a ship is one plying in salt water, the bottom of the ship, the rudder and sea connections are examined with the ship in drydock annually.
(d)	Where a ship is one plying in fresh water, the bottom of the ship, the rudder and sea connections are examined with the ship in dock every second year or every fourth year, according to the nature of the waters in which the ship is employed.
(e)	The tailshafts are drawn for inspection at periodic intervals varying from two to four years, according to the arrangement of the shaft and the waters in which the ship is employed.
2.	The organization of the steamship inspection service provides for thirty-two steamship inspectors.
The extent to which passenger vessels are inspected is given in answer to question No.
3.	A passenger boat with a carrying capacity of 1.000 passengers might have lifeboat equipment for less than 200 persons. She
Questions

would, however, have other equipment in the way of buoyant apparatus or life rafts, which, with the boats, would provide for a certain percentage of the total complement, ranging from 100 per cent to 40 per cent, according to whether the vessel were employed in open waters or sheltered waters. Every ship is required to carry a lifejacket for each person on board.

subtopic: LETTER CARRIER SERVICE
speechtext:
1. The main factors governing the inauguration of letter carrier service are: (a) population to be served; (b) postal revenue collected;

(c) density of population; (d) postal accommodation for carrying on business; (e) time of arrival of mails; (f) local improvements, such as, sidewalks, receptacles for the receipt of mails, labelling of streets, numbering of houses, etc.
There is no hard and fast rule as regards postal revenue collected or population to be served. The department does endeavour to restrict the inauguration of letter carrier delivery to points where the revenue is approximately $30,000 and the population 10,000.
There are, however, cases where due to the exigencies of the service, letter carrier delivery has been established at points where these limits have not been met.

Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to address a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). I notice advertisements in this morning's papers for an issue of government bonds to the amount of $85,000,000. Is the minister prepared to make a statement touching the matter, or to give any information in relation to it?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to advise me of his question, and I have a statement prepared in the matter which I believe should be made to the house.
The $S5,000,000 dominion government loan which is advertised in the morning papers is being offered for the purpose of redeeming the $89,787,000 five per cent war loan bonds which mature on March 1 next. The new issue will take the form of $30,000,000 seven-year 21 per cent bonds dated January 15, 1937, and maturing January 15, 1944, priced to the public at 99J and accrued interest, to yield approximately 2-327 per cent; and $55,000,000 thirty-year 3 per cent bonds dated January 15. 1937, and maturing January 15, 1967, priced to the public at 98 and accrued interest, to yield approximately 3-10 per cent. The seven-j-ear bonds are redeemable at par as a whole at the option of the government on or after January 15, 1943, upon thirty days'

notice, and the thirty-year bonds are redeemable in whole or in part at the option of the government on any interest payment date upon sixty days' notice at the following prices:
On or prior to January 15, 1942, at 105; thereafter
to and including January 15, 1947, at 104; thereafter
to and including January 15, 1952 at 103; thereafter
to and including January 15, 1957 at 102; thereafter
to and including January 15, 1962 at 101; and thereafter
at par.
In keeping with our general policy, it was considered advisable to make it possible for the dominion to call the thirty-year bonds at any time during the life of the bonds.
The war loan bonds which mature on March 1, and which are to be paid off out of the proceeds of this issue, together with a certain amount of cash from the dominion treasury, are payable in New York and Canada, and it is believed that a very large percentage of the bonds are now held in the United States. As a Canadian offering would have necessitated a very difficult, if not an impossible, exchange transfer problem, the new bonds are being offered in the United States and will be payable in legal tender currency of the United States. The new issue has been registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Washington, under the United States Securities Act of 1933. the registration statement having become effective to-day.
The new issue is being offered by an underwriting syndicate under the leadership of Morgan Stanley and Company and consisting of thirty-nine other underwriting houses including a number of Canadian investment dealers.
It will be recalled that the 5 per cent war loan bonds which are being retired by the new issue represent one of the two remaining tax-free issues of the dominion government. The other tax-free issue is the $236,209,800 5J per cent victory loan which matures on December 1 next, and which we intend to refund by means of an issue payable in Canada only. We expect, therefore that the year 1937 will see the last of Canada's tax-free bond issues which were floated during the war period.
The rates obtained on the new issue in New York represent, I believe, the lowest rates ever obtained for a Canadian bond offering of comparable maturities in that market. It will be apparent that the new offering will residt in a substantial saving to

Purchasing Power-Mr. Hayhurst
the dominion treasury, not only because of the reduction of nearly $2,000,000 in annual interest charges, but also because of the increase in income tax revenue as a result of the elimination of the tax-free feature.
The house will be interested to know that reports from New York this morning indicate that the sale of the issue is proceeding very satisfactorily.

subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege on this occasion to take part in this vital and important debate. Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) said that Houdini on the stage took rabbits out of a hat, but Houdini could not make a living by selling rabbits. In this kind of language he attempts to suggest that our proposals involving a new economic system are based upon juggling tactics. There is Houdini-like juggling taking place to-day, but it is done by the financiers. They juggle money to please themselves, irrespective of the productive capacity of the nation. Houdini made his living by fooling the public; to-day the financial wizards make their living by doing likewise. They take the profit out of the medium we call money and credit, a medium which should not be based upon a profit motive, but which should be the blood stream of human society. The arguments of yesterday seemed to me to fail because they did not recognize that money should be the servant of mankind and not its master Today we are worshipping the golden calf almost as effectively as it was worshipped in days of old.
For instance, the price of gold has been fixed at a certain point. We know that today gold is worth around $35 per ounce. It is thus made profitable for the gold producers to take great chances in finding new fields. Gold is a metal of intrinsic worth and value, but it should not have such a tremendous importance in our monetary system. If the price of gold can be fixed at $35 per ounce, why should) not the price of wheat, of beef, or of other necessities of life be fixed at an equal standard1 of value? We sell wheat at twenty cents per bushel and at $1.20 per bushel, which on the face of it is an utter absurdity. Some of my hon. friends no doubt think that this wheat must be exported and sold on a market which will depress the price according to the export value of the wheat. Under the new economics we recognize that wheat and other commodities are as valuable



Purchasing Power-Mr. Hayhurst
as gold, nickel, platinum, copper or any other metal. These commodities should have an intrinsic value and worth, and the productive capacity of mankind should not be drastically curtailed by financiers who feel that the piling up of goods is necessarily an extravagance on the part of the people. We cannot build a superstructure on a rotten foundation. We feel that the new economic problem we are facing to-day is something which has been built upon our capital structure. In our anxiety to make the world safe for democracy it is a matter of real urgency that we do not tip the baby out with the bath water.
We realize the capitalism as it exists today can be made to operate both ways, for the good of mankind or for the destruction of mankind. Some people are advocating the discarding of capitalism, but I believe that that is moving too fast. Democracy must be made safe for the individual. Yesterday the hon. member for Huron North was suggesting that we might purchase the Royalite oil wells in Alberta or the Noranda mines in Quebec. That is not the principle of social credit. The principle of social credit is to give back to the people and to the government the absolute control of money, credit and currency. These should be taken away from private individuals, from the banking system as it exists to-day. We are not advocating the ownership of any productive machinery because we believe that if the capitalistic system were made to work for the welfare of mankind it would be quite capable of producing wealth in abundance.
Some people say that we should be niggardly and save in order to buy more bonds with which our country would be put more into debt. I think we might as well attempt to save acorns instead of planting them to grow into great oaks. The capitalistic system of to-day is capable of producing wealth in abundance, therefore we feel that a new economic or monetary system, should be established to take care of that tremendous production, irrespective of booms and depressions. This new system would take care of the welfare of all our people, not only those who are blind or who were wounded overseas in the great war. Everyone would be taken care of irrespective of class and position in life. The people are the basis of the wealth of a nation.
We feel that we should creep before we walk. We are not out to destroy capitalism. We are not communists, neither are we followers of the nazi doctrine. We believe in an economic democracy, but we contend that money should be controlled by the people. Many questions are asked as to

whether sufficient can be produced in this country. I am reminded of the proverb, "consistency, thou art a jewel." I feel that at all times we should be consistent. It is a wrong management of money that restricts production. If we save up or regiment our men to be soldiers and then deliberately sabotage not only the national wealth but man power through international rivalries brought about by the continual struggle for markets and credits abroad, then I say that civilization is doomed.
I feel that we should establish in our minds a wealth creating philosophy as opposed to a debt creating philosophy. Our country is not poor except in terms of money. There is not another country in the world more richly endowed by nature than Canada. Yet here in Canada we find thousands of people who believe in the so-called orthodox economics of scarcity, when in fact the productive capacity of the country is capable of supplying all the needs of her citizens. Many have said that inflation will ruin our nation, but a study of the situation proves that it is deflation rather than inflation that is the cause of untold poverty, distress and suffering. We do not wish for inflation. A shower is better than a flood.
Some say that this creative money would pile up and never be cancelled. It is an extraordinary thing that the same people never complain of a. system under which debt piles up and is never cancelled. At the present time we have a debt economics, but if our money represented the produced wealth of the country we would have a wealth economics, which would in time balance or distribute our debt. There was an old saying of the pioneers on this great North American continent : We raise more grain to feed more hogs to get more money to buy more land to raise more grain to feed more hogs to get more money to buy more land, and so on. It is ridiculous to think that such are the actual conditions in Canada to-day. Here we are consuming less in order to increase our ability to produce more in order to consume less in order to increase our ability to produce more. Surely the old philosophy of tightening one's belt should not prevail in the civilized world to-day when mankind by advancement in technological skill is now able to produce wealth in abundance. Imagine telling people to-day to tighten their belts, to increase their capacity to produce more by consuming less. It is an absolute necessity that purchasing power should be put into the hands of the consumers in order that the consuming capacity will more nearly equal the productive capacity of mankind.

Purchasing Power-Mr. Hayhurst
We have struggled for our liberty in this great empire of ours. We have struggled for the liberty of the individual, and we are no longer slaves. We and our ancestors have fought in order that we may be free men. Our ancestors have struggled in the past and we have continued to struggle for political liberty, for political enfranchisement, for the right to vote. We have won these privileges, and the result is that to-day most of our people have the right to vote, except in the province of Quebec, across the river from here, where they still recognize women as in the same class as the insane and the Indians and have not yet seen the necessity of giving women the vote as persons.
We have struggled for our political freedom and we hold it dear. We have fought for our individual freedom and enjoy that freedom to-day. But we are now facing a greater fight than ever. We are facing a fight for financial freedom and economic liberty. We are now asking that the government exercise the power which they have to create their own credits and take away that power from those who exercise it to-day, further that the government issue those credits free of interest and free of the profit motive. As I said at the outset, money and credit are the blood-stream of society, and if the profit motive is allowed to stay in this great blood-stream of society, civilization itself will fall.
It has been suggested by some that we should be hard, that we should train and discipline our people to be soldiers. They tell us to go back to the old days of the pioneers who ploughed and sowed and reaped, using their own muscular energy and earning their living by the sweat of their brow. But, Mr. Speaker, I say that we shall not see such conditions again. You remember Longfellow's description of the village blacksmith:
The smith, a mighty man is he,
With large and sinewy hands.
In how many villages in Canada do you find the smith to-day? His day is past, and it is impossible for us to think of going back to the days of the pioneers and using their ancient methods. To-day is the day of farm machinery, of technological advancement and great productive capacity; the methods of the old pioneering days are gone forever. The scientific and inventive genius of man has solved our production problem by devising better methods, and we feel that the financial system should now reflect our greater productive capacity.
31111-10}
Before I close I should like to give a quotation from Professor Irving Fisher's book, from which my leader quoted yesterday, " 100% Money." Mr. Hemphill, in his introduction, says:
Our statesmen have consistently declined to study this question and provide a sound monetary system, an adequate permanent currency, scientifically calculated to expand consistently with our increasing population and our increasing ability to produce.
Somehow, the intelligent public of this nation must learn the fundamentals of this question. We can no longer depend upon our banking system to furnish all the money we have to do business with. The principal reason this depression continues is that the banks are not lending, and as a result, the money with which to expand business does not exist. It is so simple that business men largely overlook this fundamental situation and continue to search for some economic "fourth dimension" to explain our distressing situation, but there is no mysterious force defeating our efforts to exchange goods and services. We haven't the money nor any substitute in circulation, and that is the essence of the story.
In Professor Fisher's book, he presents in lucid detail the operation of this erratic banking-monetary system, and the obvious remedy. It is the most important subject intelligent persons can investigate and reflect upon. It is so important that our present civilization may collapse unless it is widely understood and the defects remedied very soon.
It is your problem and mine.
There are probably many, sir, in this new era upon which we have entered who blindly refuse to recognize that great truth. We must remember that if evolution is not allowed to proceed in an orderly way, if it is dammed up first at one point and then at another, the same forces that make for evolutionary progress will likely blast a way by revolutionary methods. And so, Mr. Speaker, we hope that the House of Commons and the people of Canada will give earnest consideration to these new questions which are facing them. The main question before us to-day is who is to control the future monetary policy of this country, and shall not the profit motive be taken away and the credit of the nation be used for the welfare of the people of the country!
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops): In rising to speak to this resolution I may say that I am not an advocate of Mr. Aberhart or of Mr. Douglas, nor am I a supporter of social credit. But I do not believe that this resolution is social credit. I have long been of the opinion that some kind of monetary reform is overdue. I am a Liberal, but not because I believe that Liberalism is a cure for all our troubles. Nor do I believe that party government is a cure-all. It is my

Purchasing Power-Mr. O'Neill
view that if democracy is to survive we must have party government, but I hold that if the principles of the Liberal party are complied with we shall be able to bring about the monetary and other reforms that are required.
The problem of unemployment is, in my opinion, nearly as acute to-day as it was when this government came into power. It is without question the outstanding problem of the times, and it is very closely allied with that of credit. Prior to the election, in fact prior to the nomination, I held practically the same views as regards monetary reform that I hold to-day, and I expressed those views not only in the Liberal party but in public. With the abundant evidence that there is on all sides of poverty and distress, I see every reason for continuing to believe in the soundness of that viewpoint. When anyone to-day dares to voice an opinion that does not coincide with that of advocates of the present so-called sound money system, he is immediately held up to the most belittling ridicule and the most withering sarcasm. I regret that during this debate there has not been shown a little more of the Liberal principle of toleration.
To illustrate the point I am trying to make: during the year 1930 it seemed advisable to the then government that a loan should be floated for the purpose of refunding. I have no intention at this time of criticizing the government of that day, because I believe that any other government would have done the same thing under this system. They required a loan of some hundred million dollars for the purpose of refunding. Not being very sure of the feeling of the people at that time, the premiers of ihe nine different provinces, together with the then acting prime minister, went on the radio as supersalesmen, so to speak, to sell this bond issue to the people of Canada, and without exception, I believe, one of the points they stressed was the wonderful opportunity for a safe investment that that loan presented to our people. It was safe, they said, for the reason that it was backed not only by the government but by all the natural resources of this wonderful dominion. The point is that if it is necessaiy to put up the natural resources of the country as collateral security to guarantee a loan, why does the bank not belong to the people? Why is it necessary to pay a tribute to some private individual in order that we may be able to use something that belongs to us?-because in the last analysis what we are using is the public credit.

I am just as thoroughly convinced as I was prior to the election that if we continue to pile up obligations for public purposes as we are now doing, it cannot but inevitably result in the total collapse of our present financial structure, with all the chaos, misery and privation that will follow such an event. On the other hand if we change the system to one of public ownership of the right to issue currency and credit, I see no reason why there should be any repudiation of the just responsibilities that we have assumed. I believe those responsibilities can all be met, but they cannot be met if we continue to finance as we are doing at the present time.

subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I notice that this resolution states:
That, in the opinion of this house, the Canadian government should consider the advisability of beginning this year to issue purchasing power, and to use that purchasing power for the improvement of the economic condition of the Canadian people.
In rising to support the motion I do so with certain qualifications. In the first place I should like to make it quite plain that, so far as I understand social credit, either of the Aberhart or	of	the	Douglas	variety, theresolution is	not	either one of	the two. Itproposes the	use of	national	credit rather
than any system of social credit. I compliment the leader of the social credit party on being broadminded enough to bring forward a proposal which I feel is in line with Liberal policy, rather than a straightforward proposal of definite social credit according to either Aberhart or Douglas.
One of the things I would quarrel with in the wording	of	the	resolution	is the suggestion that the government should consider the advisability of "beginning" this year to issue purchasing power. I have spoken in the house on this question on several occasions and indicated that in my opinion we have done this very thing more than once in the past. I shall refer to the occasions when I think we have done that very thing, and if I support the resolution it is because I think there will be no harm in giving some study to a further understanding of some of the things we have done in the past with no evil results of any kind so far as I can see. You may say, when have we ever issued purchasing power without somebody giving value for it? The first occasion that will occur to those who know anything about the dominion is that up to 1913 we issued thirty million dollars' worth of dominion notes which were legal tender in this country against a gold reserve of one-quarter

Purchasing Power-Mr. Tucker
of that amount. In other words, with gold worth roughly a little Over seven millions, we issued and used as a government thirty million dollars' worth of money; that is, we put out that much purchasing power and placed it in the hands of the people. Shortly after the outbreak of war we raised that amount from thirty to fifty millions, and, on a gold basis of one-quarter of fifty million dollars, were actually putting out purchasing power for the use of the government to the extent of three-fourths of that fifty mtdion dollars, with nothing whatever behind it except the law itself and without employing means of taxation or otherwise to raise the money. I am favourable to a study of extending that principle as far as it is safe to do so without upsetting or .jeopardizing our present democratic system, the so-called capitalist system.
Another occasion on which we made use of this system was when during the great war we issued 816,000,000 worth of our legal tender against dominion railway securities. As the railways had done many times in the past, they came to Ottawa wanting the government, as I suppose, to guarantee another bond issue. The government of that day thought that they would try an experiment, and instead of guaranteeing a bond issue and making themselves liable to pay interest on it, they said to the railways, "You deposit your bonds with us and we will print $16,000,000 worth of money and lend it to you." I asked certain questions in the House of Commons last session in regard to this matter. First, I asked:
Have the railway obligations or securities against which $16,000,000 of dominion notes were issued pursuant to authority contained in An Act respecting the issue of Dominion notes. Statutes of Canada, 1915, Chap. 4 been paid?
The answer was "no." So that the money is still owing the government of the country. Next I asked:
If so, when were they paid?
The reply was that this was answered1 by No. 1. Next:
How much interest, if any, has been paid on said securities to date?
The answer was:
Interest paid by the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company on advances secured by the obligations referred to amounted to $2 327 -945.23.
The next question was:
To whom was such interest paid?
The answer was that it was paid to the Receiver General of Canada. Now that is a different story altogether from many of the other things that have had to be told in
this house. Instead of the country having to pay interest on railway financing, we find that the government itself lent money to the railways-money that cost it nothing except the cost of printing-and on which it has collected to date over $2,000,000. Nothing bad has happened in consequence of that; and if instead of paying interest we can collect interest, I ask every hon. member in this house, why should we be afraid to investigate further the possibility of extending such a system of carrying on the affairs of the country?
Not only at this time did we finance the railways to the extent of $16,000,000, but at the same time the government gave itself $10,000,000 for the purpose of carrying on business. In other words, the government made an issue of $16,000,000 against railway securities a.nd $10,000,000 just on its own securities and it has used that money without resorting to taxation to get it or borrowing and having to pay interest on it.
There is another instance of the issue by the government of this country of purchasing power without first falling back upon taxation or borrowing to get it. I would refer the house to the emergency issue, during the war, against British treasury bills of $50,000,000 for the purpose of buying goods in Canada required by the British government. That was issued solely against British treasury bills. I do not know what rate of interest these British treasury bills carried, but I assume that they carried some rate of interest. These bills were finally paid off in 1927 and, I assume, they were paid off both as to principal and with whatever interest they bore at the time. In other words, we issued $50,000,000 of purchasing power, we stimulated Canadian industry when we did so, and at the same time we collected not only that $50,000,000 but interest on the money. If that is not good business, then I must admit that there is something wrong with my reasoning in the matter.
Let us take another instance in which this policy was followed. We find that under the Finance Act the same method was adopted. The government issued to the banks printed money against dominion government bonds; and any one who will read the Canadian Macmillan report can find the statement as to the amount issued from time to time by the dominion government of money against which the only security that was pledged consisted of dominion government bonds and the guarantee of the banks who pledged them. There was no gold behind it, and there was no limit to the amount of money that could be issued under the Finance Act. They could have issued billions of dollars had they seen

Purchasing Power-Mr. Tucker
fit. Under the Finance Act in July, 1933, the government of Canada had in issue $48,000,000 worth of good legal currency against the bonds of the country and they were collecting interest from the banks on that issue of currency * again, very good business and something which it would do us no harm to study.
As a further instance of the issue of purchasing power, mav I point out that under the last administration there was a change in the Dominion Notes Act which came into force on June 30, 1934. We provided that the backing of our dominion notes should be twenty-five per cent gold, and on the basis of that amount of gold the last administration, led by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), increased the dominion notes printed by the dominion government by $53,000,000. I well remember following the discussion of this matter in the press at that time. This money was being used to pay ordinary expenses of government, and many believe that if the government issues money it is a dangerous thing, but that the banks can inflate and expand credit to any extent and no harm is done. Such were wondering what was going to happen to the public financial structure when, as I say, the government led by the present leader of the opposition was so bold as to issue this flood of new money. Well, what happened? Nothing of any distressing consequence. One of the things that happened was that by the end of the following year bank deposits in Canada had risen by $250,000,000. That is to say, there was that much more money to do business with in Canada. Had that policy been followed carefully I think we would have come out of the depression much sooner. I make bold to say that had the leader of the opposition had the courage of his apparent convictions at that time, had he followed that policy instead of the advice of some of his friends in the cabinet, perhaps we would have come out of the depression to a greater extent under his administration than we actually did.
Let us take another example of the issuing of purchasing power by an institution of our own creation. I refer to the Bank of Canada. We have provided by statute that the Bank of Canada may go and buy a dollar's worth of gold and, on the strength of that, issue four dollars' worth of Bank of Canada bills which are legal tender. In other words, it can take one million dollars' worth of gold and with it provide itself with four million dollars' worth of purchasing power. It may be said that this is not of any advantage to the government of the country. I contend that under the Bank of Canada Act, if that policy were followed to a sane extent, of

course, any profits it made therefrom over and above running expenses and dividends on shares would came back to the government of the country. The only quarrel I have with the Bank of Canada is that it is not making use of its power. According to the last statement of the Bank of Canada it had on hand, in round figures, $179,000,000 worth of gold. On the strength of that it could have issued roughly $716,000,000 worth of legal tender and still have been within what is recognized all over the world as the safe limit. According to the last statement of the bank it actually had in issue $134,000,000 worth of notes. In other words with the gold the Bank of Canada has on hand at the present time it could issue $582,000,000 of new money and have that money amply secured according to the best judgment of the nations when last they considered the matter in conference.
The question any ordinary layman will ask is this: Why keep the gold and make no use of it in a country such as Canada, while at the same time you are forced to borrow money internally with which to do internal work and redeem internal debt? I suggest that if that $582,000,000 were issued by the bank and loaned to this dominion to pay on its debt a large sum of money would be saved in interest alone. According to the last Canada Year Book the average interest rate on dominion indebtedness was 4*136 per cent. That would not be quite so high to-day, but for purposes of calculation if we say the rate is 4 per cent, the saving to this country wrould be $23,000,000 in interest alone.
The question we must ask ourselves is this: If we can do that and keep within the limits of sound finance, why do we not do it? The answer always given is, "If we put out that much legal tender and increased our cash reserves to that extent, with the tendency that has grown up on the part of the banks to lend to the extent of ten times the amount of the cash reserves in the country, it would mean a tremendous inflation of credit." The first thing I should like to say in that connection is this: I do not say this amount should be issued all at once. I say we should start and go far enough to bring about some inflation of credit in order to put our young people to work, to develop our great natural resources and to provide some of the things this country needs. An inflation of credit for that purpose would do no harm.
I am reminded of what Germany has done during the last three years. According to the ideas of the orthodox economist Germany wiped out the savings of her people by her policy of uncontrolled inflation, which

Purchasing Power-Mr. Tucker
destroyed the value of her monetary unit. That was not a case of the controlled issue of currency; it was a deliberate issuance of money until the value of that currency was destroyed. The question that strikes one is this: Where is Germany borrowing the money to-day with which to do the vast amount of internal work that is being carried on there, when under that hypothesis the savings of her people were wiped out? Someone in this house may say, "Oh, but Germany wants credit from foreign nations." Germany does want credit with which to buy abroad. Because of her vast armament program she cannot possibly produce and export enough goods to pay for the things she needs to carry on that program, but so far as the internal development of Germany is concerned, she does not want to borrow money from anyone externally. Germany is using every bit of her natural resources to the very limit, as she is using her labour power, her people. It is all very well for us to say that they are not making as great a success of it as we might. I say that Canada, with her tremendous resources, with a population just as able and intelligent as the people of Germany, might well embark on a policy of expansion which would put our unemployed to work. When Germany can embark upon a policy of rearmament which has cost four billions dollars; when Germany can build military roads some of which cost over a hundred thousand dollars a mile to construct; when Germany is making such full use of all her resources, largely I suggest by the use of national credit, I say to this House of Commons that, with our great natural resources, we have no right to say that we will not even consider the possibility of embarking on a policy of expansion, peaceful of course, on a similar basis of use of national credit.
We live in a world of land hungry nations, Mr. Speaker. On the one hand we have countries such as Germany using every ounce of their natural resources, while on the other hand we are not making use of our young unemployed people to develop our great natural resources. In past years we have permitted our young men and women to drift away to the United States, and we are afraid to have people come to our land in order to help develop this great empty country of ours for fear of aggravating the unemployment situation. Our forefathers pioneered this country and placed it in our hands, but we, by refusing to develop it, are fairly tempting the attack of some more powerful nation that thinks it can make better use of our resources than we are making. That
is one of the things that we, representing the Canadian people, have to bear in mind. If as a Canadian people we are not prepared to make use of the natural resources that providence placed within our borders for the benefit not only of ourselves but of all those who wish to come to our shores, and we feel we should properly admit then we are courting the risk of having these lands wrenched away from us some time in the future-perhaps distant-when the pressure of population becomes much greater in some of the overcrowded countries.
Those who simply say that what we have had in the past is good enough, so that we need not examine any new idea, are not being fair to the people who in the past took chances in order to found this land of ours. If there is a sign that this credit inflation is going further than it should, it will be very easy to stop. Under the law at the present time the chartered banks must deposit with the Bank of Canada five per cent of the amount of their deposits. If, when we put out more currency-which does not cost us anything and which bears no interest-we find that the banks are going too far in their policy of credit inflation, we can give the government power to require the banks to deposit more of their own deposits with the Bank of Canada than five per cent. That would cut down such inflation. Let the government take over in that way the absolute power over the issuance of credit by the banks in this country. This will be much more effective than the power we have given it of buying and selling bills. So I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is a possibility of using over $500,000,000 worth of money without a cent of cost to the country, and that we could easily control any tendency to overinflation that might result. Take again the example of Germany. That country came through a terrible war, into which it put all its resources, and in which it was beaten. It came through a revolution, but it has reestablished itself to on amazing extent largely by the use of national credit. Surely with the experts we have in our government, they could see to it that if we made use of this power it would not be abused by the banks or by anyone else. At any rate I have that much confidence in the leaders of Canadian banking and finance.
The next case to which I should like to refer, Mr. Speaker, is this: The time we used our national credit when the present leader of the opposition was in power. He borrowed $35,000,000 from the banks on treasury bills and had the banks take those

Purchasing Power-Mr. Tucker
bills to the Minister of Finance, who had printed and who issued against those bills
S35.000.000 worth of new money, under the provisions of the Finance Act. In that case we actually paid the banks four per cent interest, and the Minister of Finance charged the banks three per cent interest, so as a result that 135,000,000 cost us one per cent. That was an example of the use of national credit. I have never heard of any harm resulting from that action, and if any harm did come from it I should like to hear about it from responsible people. If no harm has come from it, why should it not be used more extensively?-of course now through the Bank of Canada.
We have authorized the banks to issue purchasing power, by virtue of the powers already given them. I have heard doubts expressed by some people as to whether or not the banks actually issue or create purchasing power. I have before me the first report of the Bank of Canada, and at page 9 I find the following:
Adding to the deposit figure $40,497,965 in Bank of Canada notes, which the banks held in their tills, we find the total cash reserves at December 31, 1935, were $222,133,998, equal to approximately ten per cent of the chartered bank's deposit liabilities in Canada.
Incidentally I am sometimes told that in a system of governmental finance the use of national credit would depend upon the confidence of the people. I submit the people of Canada have just as much confidence in the integrity and solvency of the Dominion of Canada as they have in any bank in Canada. I submit further that the working of our present system depends upon the confidence of the people in the banking system of Canada, because if the deposit liabilities of the banks in Canada are to-day ten times the amount of the actual cash reserves in the country, in the event of the people suddenly asking for their money on deposit from the banks they would receive only about ten cents on the dollar. If banks in Canada can safely do business on that basis, surely the nation can do it on the same basis.
When we read the opinions of people interested in the matter we find one view in one book and another in another. I believe one can gain no great amount of profit from citing opinions of writers of books, because each writer has his own opinion and it is hard to weight the value of each writer's opinion. Possibly the opinion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is worth more than those of writers of some books.

I read from page 44 of the report, because I believe the question under consideration does not receive the careful thought it should receive:
If a bank receives from some new or outside source an increase in its "cash reserves," it will in the ordinary course of events proceed to make loans or to buy securities. The public receiving the proceeds of the loans or sales will deposit in the banks all that they do not require for hand-to-hand cash. In so far as these deposits are made in other banks, cheques wili be drawn on the original bank, with the effect of diminishing its reserves and increasing those of its competitors. The latter, provided their cash position be already satisfactory, will then be in a position to make additional loans and investments, if conditions warrant, and this in turn will enable the public to make further deposits. In so far as the loans and investments made by the original bank return to it as deposits, it will be in a position to make further loans or investments. Through this process of lending, investing and depositing, the increased cash reserve is distributed among the banks and the volume of loans and investments and deposits is increased by an amount several times greater than the amount of the original increase in cash reserves.
In other words if the government of Canada through the Bank of Canada lends a bank a million dollars, on the strength of that loan the bank may turn around and buy government bonds to the extent of several times that million dollars. There can be no question about that; as an authority I offer the findings of the royal commission.

Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) will forgive me I am sure if I do not seek to traverse the ground he has covered in his very interesting speech. I imagine it is needless for me to tell the house that I do not speak to this resolution as an expert on monetary questions. I have studied some of these questions for a number of years and I have nothing but envy for those who are able to discuss them with apostolic certainty.
It seems to me that at this time we must address ourselves to the exact wording of the resolution before the house. The resolution is couched in these terms:
That, in the opinion of this house, the Canadian government should consider the advisability of beginning this year to issue purchasing power, and to use that purchasing power for the improvement of the economic condition of the Canadian people.
As to the latter portion of the resolution I am sure there is no difference of opinion among the various groups in this house. We are all most anxious to improve the economic condition of the Canadian people. I would also say that I share the views expressed by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill), that the existing banking and

monetary system should not be sacrosanct and unchangeable. There have already been some far-reaching changes, not only in the system but in our views regarding it. Obviously as we move forward toward new social objectives we must fashion the instruments of state to meet these new objectives.
In approaching this particular question I am bound to say that I am influenced by certain principles which to my mind have been established in the experience of this country. I cannot conceive of a purchasing power in any real sense apart from the production of goods and services. In a primitive community this was self-evident. You exchanged goods and services and as goods and services were produced you increased the store of purchasing power. Therefore I cannot conceive that it lies within the power of the dominion government to issue purchasing power. It is within the power of the dominion government, or of any government, to create conditions under which the people may themselves increase purchasing power. I may say that that has been the purpose of all governments in this country, however different their policies may have been.
I was much interested a moment ago when the hon. member for Kamloops referred to the unemployment situation in British Columbia. It is within his knowledge and within the knowledge of every member of this house that within the past year there has been a very considerable improvement in the economic condition of British Columbia. That improvement was not brought about by the issue of money purchasing power; it was brought about by the creation of conditions under which the people of British Columbia were enabled to increase their purchasing power in terms of production of goods and services. As a result of several trade agreements-the trade agreement between this country and Great Britain, the trade agreement between this country and the United States, and the settlement of differences between this country and Japan-barriers were removed which theretofore had prevented the free flow of trade, and as these barriers were removed there was an expansion of trade. New markets were established; as a result there was a greater degree of industrial activity and therefore a greater production of goods and services, and the income of the people of British Columbia was increased.

You may issue dominion notes, you may expand credit, you may establish titles to goods and services; but let us assume, for example, to take the case of British Columbia, that you had not had created the conditions which resulted in a stimulus of industry, but that in that province in the same period of time you had merely had an issue of dominion notes to this or that extent. Can it be suggested for one moment that the condition of the people of British Columbia, with the issue of purchasing power in terms of currency, would have been as good as it is with the additional purchasing power through the production of goods and services? That is the point, Mr. Speaker, which it does seem to me is vital in the consideration of this question. My point is that essentially the real income of a community consists of the goods and services that it produces, and we are therefore compelled in considering any question of currency inflation to determine how far such a policy is likely to go in its ultimate effect in increasing or decreasing the productive power of the country.
It so happened that following the late war I spent some time in central Europe when the countries there were in the midst of an inflationary boom. I am far from suggesting that there was not an acceleration of production through the inflation of currency, but it was temporary; it was the kind of fever that precedes total collapse, and I do not think anyone who visited those countries at that time could fail to be impressed by the very serious results which followed a policy of that kind.
As I understand this resolution, it proposes, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has just said, the issue of purchasing power in terms either of pocket-book money, as explained by the hon. member for Lethbridge or, as he termed it, cheque-book money. subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
First of all I should like to say that we in this group are thoroughly in favour of the present House of Commons considering ways and means of increasing the purchasing power of the Canadian people. Neither the resolution nor the mover of the resolution (Mr. Blackmore) sets forth any specific or definite manner in which that could be done; and although the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has just read what Mr. Aberhart had to say, the members who have so far spoken in support of this resolution have not placed that very definite interpretation upon it. Therefore I take it that members of this house who do not agree with Mr. Aberhart, who do not believe that the proposals he has made in Alberta are soundly based, nevertheless have the right and the privilege to support the resolution.
There can be no question of the necessity of finding a solution of this very evident paradox of poverty and want in the midst of real and potential plenty. If evidence were lacking, we receive it every day in the House of Commons, and in the speeches that have been made in support of this resolution much confirmatory evidence can be found. The question, as we of this group see it, is how we can meet the present need and proceed to a permanent cure, and it is from that point of view that I wish to discuss the resolution. In doing so I am speaking on behalf of this group and the movement that it represents. Unfortunately, a lack of knowledge of economics-quite understandable in a country such as the one in which we live- and a great deal of very loose thinking in connection with these matters, are leading us into all kinds of by-paths. The unemployed, the distressed farmer, the idle professional man or the bankrupt business man have put their hands into their pockets and have said, " Our trouble is that we have no money." Let us bear in mind that the basic fact of man's struggle with nature is not the fact of money but the fact of producing and using things, in other words, production and consumption. Monetary devices are means which modern men have brought into use-what for? For accounting and reckoning and delivering goods and services. It is the accountancy system within the economic structure in which we live, and many people,
Purchasing Power-Mr. Coldwell

I am afraid, forget this fact. They mistake the shadow of money for the substance of things, and consequently we have a tremendous emphasis placed upon that angle of our difficulty.
I think we may say that money, in a broad sense, becomes to the possessor a readily exchangeable title to goods that have been made or services that may be rendered; and since everybody under the present system does not and cannot produce, though everybody needs to consume, we have money in order that such people may obtain the things which they need to consume at given times and in given places. Hence it follows that if in our society

and I commend this particularly to my hon. friends to the left-some persons consume without producing, they must consume some things which others have produced; and to my hon. friends to the right, let me say that in a capitalist society those who live by rent, interest and profit acquire quantities of goods or titles to goods which they have not produced but which someone else has had to produce. Increase in purchasing power among the great masses of the people, which I take to be the object of this resolution, must result in proportionately lessened returns to someone, and as far as we in this group are concerned, we clearly recognize that as a fundamental fact and we make no apologies for advocating that the lessened return shall go to that group which, through its power, has been able to accumulate vast hoards and stores of wealth. We thus face that fact quite honestly and sincerely and are prepared to disagree with those who disagree with us; we shall nevertheless continue to work consistently toward that end.
A moment ago I used the word "profit. " For the sake of clearing up any discussion which may arise on that point, may I say that I am using that term in a strictly narrow sense. Viewed in the narrow sense, "profit," I think, includes rent and interest and is the essential return which accrues to persons or groups of persons as a result of their ownership of the means of production. Let us bear this constantly in mind when we discuss the matter of profit. I do not mean, when I speak of profit, that further amount added to the price of goods which represents the cost of handling, the services of the man or woman handling the product, and so on. I do not include in the word, therefore, the cost of distribution. And again let me emphasize that you cannot increase the purchasing power of one group unless you take potential purchasing power from some other group. But, it may be said, production progressively increases. That

may be true, but the relative truth of the statement that I have just made is, I believe, plain, and no manipulation-if I may use that word-of currency or credit can falsify that position.
To argue that a form of purchasing power that we call credit is an intangible thing is,
I think, to be quite oblivious to the fact that money in any form is a title to goods and services, the fruit of someone's labour, and that such goods are quite tangible. These goods cannot be created, as is sometimes inferred at the point of a fountain pen, although they may be monetized, represented by figures, through a fountain pen; and I believe that if we could get into our minds very clearly the distinction between goods and money we should have a little less confusion in discussing this important question of finance. I am not saying that bankers cannot and do not create credit; they do. But they create it on assets that may be hypothecated to them; in other words behind the creation we have goods. It may be said, in the example given this afternoon of the government issuing notes, that this was different, that nothing was hypothecated. But I would point out that something was hypothecated. When fifteen, or twenty, or two hundred millions of new dollar titles were issued by the Dominion of Canada that meant that two hundred millions' worth of labour and natural resources would ultimately validate these titles; and somewhere in the economic process that amount would have to be accounted for.
The power we have given the bankers gives them enormous power over our economic structure. Last year we of this group sought to impress upon the house the necessity of taking that power from the bankers and so we introduced a resolution asking for the national ownership of the central Bank of Canada and the chartered banks. Nor am I denying that by the wrong use of this power great economic difficulties and dislocations may arise. They do. Scientific control of our financial system-and we are in thorough agreement with those members of the house who advocate it-undoubtedly would assist in meeting some of the difficulties that are arising. For myself I would be glad under certain circumstances to see a government embark upon a mild inflationary program, but in supporting such a program I would admit that it was such.

I would have no hesitation in answering that question. I should say I would not go very far, because I am not an inflationist, as perhaps the house will see when I proceed a little further with my remarks.
We hear a great deal about sound money, and perhaps this will answer the minister's question. In my opinion a sound monetary system implies that the total amount of all money, taking into account its velocity, shall equal the value of the goods and services, priced and to be distributed by it. The nearer you can get to that the more ideal your system will be. I may say that I am not taking that definition or that statement from any radical economist. It will be found in many of our standard works on economics.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That is an orthodox
statement.

subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Yes. Too little money, or money moving too slowly, causes a deflation. On the other hand too much money or money moving too rapidly causes inflation, and both are equally bad. I sometimes accuse gentlemen who are orthodox of being deflationists. I think in reality their frame of mind is rather toward deflation than toward stabilization; and I would call some other monetary theorists frankly inflationists, and recognise them as such. Let us bear this in mind, too, that the flow of money and even the effects of inflation are very difficult to gauge. I think President Roosevelt found that out. For three years he poured billions of dollars into circulation, and it was not until after three years had passed that he began to see those signs of recovery which he sought. Even then that recovery was based, perhaps, upon factors other than the sole monetary factor which was so greatly emphasized.
The lesson of this, it seems to me, is that in order to carry out the purpose of the motion which has been introduced, many more factors are involved and many more things need to be done than some members of the house would seem to realize, if we may judge from their discussion of this question. If we are going to achieve a balanced economy we must assume some responsibility for planning production as well as for encouraging distribution. This, probably, is the point at which we part company with our friends to the left and our friends to the right. Our friends to the left want to issue quantities of titles to goods they neither own nor control, while our friends to the right support the theory of automatic self-adjustments, which tragically enough alternate between booms and depressions. We would endeavour to progress toward an ever-expanding production of goods and services and to an ever-increasing enjoyment of them.
Bearing that in mind, Mr. Speaker, you will see why a few moments ago I spoke of balancing money, tokens if you like, with goods, because that is the only way in which we shall ever achieve anything in the nature of a balanced economic structure. In order to do that, however, we must frankly recognize that we have to institute planning and quite wide measures of economic control. We contend, of course, that though steps may be taken in that direction, this can never be achieved in its entirety under the present price and profit system, because the flow of profit tends to immobilize vast quantities of purchasing power at least temporarily. There

Purchasing Power-Mr. Coldwell
you see the fundamental defect in our economic structure. What the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) said may be perfectly true, that enough purchasing power is issued to enable the goods produced to be consumed; yet always there is a dip, a taking out of a portion in the form of profit, in the economic sense in which I use that term, and as the concentration of industry and finance comes into fewer and fewer hands, that dip becomes a much more serious factor in the economic situation.
There we have the real difficulty that arises. It is the concentration of money in the hands of a few, who cannot spend it and who do not even find safe places in which to lend it, that causes disequilibrium. Were it not for these factors the process of production would itself distribute sufficient purchasing power, as the Minister of Labour has said. For in a properly planned economy if you did not distribute purchasing power in that way, you might distribute it subsequently by a social dividend. May I say to hon. members to my left that that is the only way in which they will ever achieve social dividends. Thus it ought to be apparent that purchasing power involves very much more than some of our friends in Alberta would seem to think.
This is an intricate economic subject. Every hon. member who attempts to debate it in an assembly of this kind must know that it is a difficult subject to place before a gathering. I believe that is one of the difficulties of present day discussions throughout the country concerning money and credit. For this reason I should like to place before the house a resolution passed at our conference held in Toronto last July. The resolution, which I believe summarizes our position, is in these words:
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation reiterates its policy of credit and investment control in the plainest terms.
In passing, may I observe that the matter of investment control is one to which I would like to believe the government is giving serious consideration. As I look at the stock market fluctuations from day to day I can see all the factors which operated prior to 1929. Unless an attempt is made to meet the situation we shall probably see stocks go higher than they did in that year, and the crash will be just that much greater. The following paragraphs are these:
(l_). Central Bank. We demand the complete elimination of all private ownership and control from the Bank of Canada.
(2). Commercial Banks. Useful as it is, the Bank of Canada is not a sufficient instrument for credit control if the rest of our financial

machinery is left in the hands of big business to be used for private profit. The responsibility for directing most of the country's short-term credit rests with the commercial banks. Their credit policy accentuates booms and depressions by easing credit during "prosperity" and restricting it when business declines. Their position accentuates the present trend towards monopoly in our economy through the system of interlocking directorates which prevails between banks and large scale industrial enterprises. In addition, since their one aim is private profit and not social security, they starve us of credit for housing and other welfare services because these things do not "pay." There must be public ownership and control of the whole banking and insurance system if the credit resources of the country are to be devoted to socially useful purposes. "Social credit" parties, by ignoring this essential issue, are tending to lead our people up a blind alley.
(3)	. Long-Term Investment. In spite of many exposures of the abuses and rackets which go with the present methods of long-term financing of industry, the vital importance of this second great section of our financial machinery has not yet been brought home to the public. "Credit control" is empty talk unless accompanied by the control of investment. Private enterprise makes its big profits through stock-watering, promoters' rake-offs, directors' bonuses, transfers between interlocking companies, stock and bond speculation, artificial raising of the marketability of securities through the "investment trust," manipulation of commodity markets, and such practices. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation recognizes clearly that managed currency and credit provide only half a policy unless accompanied by drastic regulation of these practices.
A Security Board, such as recommended by the Price Spreads Commission should immediately be set up. But a far more comprehensive national investment board should also be created, as called for in the Regina manifesto in 1933. Unless this form of public control is provided, capitalist "recovery" will merely lead us into another period of hectic and unplanned expansion, with national savings invested where profits are highest and quickest instead of where social advantage is greatest, which will be followed inexorably by another and deeper depression.
(4)	. Finally, it is important to reiterate the policy laid down in our Regina manifesto in regard to the need for the social ownership of the means of production and related industries.
That, it seems to me, summarizes the position we have taken. Thus we realize there are many factors involved in the redistribution of goods and services implied in a resolution to increase purchasing power, such as the one we are now debating.
May I repeat that not the least of the important matters indicated is a security board, so that investments may go into proper productive chanels. Involved also would be fixed prices guaranteeing proper standards of living to our producers and adequate wages to our workers. Added to those factors would be the one which is per-

Purchasing Power-Mr. Coldwell
haps more important at the present time, namely the opportunity to earn money. It follows that wide measures of intelligent planning must be undertaken to replace what we regard as an outworn laissez faire economy. Let me reiterate that the problem is more complex than the mere creation of credits, and must cover the very wide field of the production and distribution of goods. Under the present system it is essentially the ownership by the bank, whether outright or by hypothecation, w7hich gives it power to control wealth, to use it, and to determine the distribution of those commodities which money is supposed to distribute.
Those people who do not own the things they need must labour to live. Either they must work, borrow or accept relief. To them existence depends upon labour, debt or dole. That, I take it, is the misfortune of our present economic situation.
If the means of production were restored to the control of society we believe that then the sum total of production could and indeed would be distributed during the process of production. If it were thought better not to do that, then any surplus accruing to the community, through community effort, could be made available in a form of subsequent social dividend. But to attempt one without the other is. in my opinion, courting economic disaster. If my view is wrong I shall be content to listen to other views. An opportunity has been provided in one of the Canadian provinces to demonstrate that my point of view is wrong, and I can assure hon. members from that province that if they succeed in demonstrating my observations this afternoon are not well founded, I shall be glad not only to admit my error but to assist them in carrying forward their experiment. If on the other hand they see that the experiment is not successful-and I submit they do-they should endeavour to work out something more nearly along the lines of economic reality.
Many will say that the point of view I have indicated involves great changes. Yes, it does, and they will come. They will not all come at once, because that would involve a tremendous and sudden dislocation. I do not believe that at the moment the best land of progress can be made in that way. Very recent history has shown that social and economic changes imply time and steps. And so I say, on behalf of the group for whom I am speaking this afternoon, we are prepared to cooperate with any other group in
this house which might not wish a fundamental change but which is ready to travel even part of the way along the road which we must eventually travel.
In conclusion may I outline some of the immediate steps which we consider to be necessary. First, the national ownership and control of the financial system. Second, the national ownership and control of monopolistic industry. Third, social security measures, including minimum wages for workers and a guaranteed minimum price for the farmer. Fourth, steeply graded income taxes with the lower brackets exempt. Fifth, progressively high death duties and inheritance taxes.
May I say that the last is a method of restoring to society as a whole the ownership of some of those things which have been taken from society by a group. I believe that this offers a painless and effective, if not a most rapid way of achieving that objective. But in imposing death duties we have no right to consider them as current revenue. We ought to consider death duties, which vary in extent from year to year, as a contribution toward the retirement of our national capital obligations.

He told them that his party did not wish to claim all the credit for the benefits they had received, that providence must be given some credit because providence had seen fit, through bad weather, to reduce production in other parts of the world. There is an instance where a man's purchasing power was not measured exactly by what he produced; his purchasing power was measured by what some one else had not produced.
I farmed for five and thirty years in western Canada. I always found that when I had a good crop,	there never seemed to be	anyprice.	When	there was a good	price, I neverseemed to have a crop. The only alternative is a dictatorship, either of the right or of the left. If the producers are to be ruined by producing the plenty which science has made possible, then the only remedy is the enforcement of artificial scarcity by means of a dictatorship. The hon. member for Huron North asked us to consider an island where only barter obtained. He told us that under such circumstances production would balance consumption. We do want to dispute that, but the hon. member did not mention such things as machinery, science, savings, investments and all the rest of it, and the price system as well. If I had the time I think I could prove that under the present price system it is impossible for industry to distribute sufficient purchasing power in order that what it produces may be sold.
Money is born as a debt. When I borrow $100, I must pay back $108. Where do those eight dollars come from? I may be told that I have produced a crop of wheat, that it comes out of the wheat deal, but that is not so. I have stooked a good many thousands of acres of wheat and I have never yet found a dollar bill in any stook. You produce wheat, you do not produce money. Savings create a shortage of purchasing power. When a man saves he refrains from consuming and to that extent goods are not sold. We are told that money saved is an investment which eventually will be paid out in wages and salaries. That may be true, but when the

money is paid out again in wages and salaries, it is paid out with respect to another cycle of production. We have two lots of goods and one lot of money, and it is impossible for one lot of money to buy two lots of goods.
Why is it that times of greatest prosperity, when everybody is working and production is at its full, are precisely the times when high pressure salesmen go around to sell their goods. It is then that it is found necessary to sell goods on time. It is because under our price system all costs must enter into prices; in those prices must be included costs which are not distributed, and it is for that reason it is impossible for industry to distribute the money which is necessary to buy what it produces. If, as the hon. member for Huron North says, production and consumption balance, I would like him to explain the ever-increasing debt. If industry were self-liquidating, as he says it is, how does he account for the ever-increasing debt not only in Canada but in all countries?
It is still doubted by some that the banks create money. There are still people who tell us that the banks lend simply what is lent to them. Now if 100 members of this chamber go to-morrow morning to a bank and each deposits a ten-dollar bill, there is $1,000. When they come out I go into the bank and I borrow $1,000. If it is true that I have borrowed the money which has just been deposited, then if they will go in and ask the manager where their money is, he will say, "I have lent it to Jaques." But the bankers do not say that. They say, "Of course, your money is here." So there you have S2,000, where only SI,000 existed before, and if that is not creation of money, what is it? I do not know. It is creation in the sense that I understand it.
We hear a good deal about inflation, and I should like to read for the benefit of those who have not done so what the originator of the system which we advocate says about inflation.

in understanding him; his writings seem perfectly straightforward to me. But then I was thoroughly deflated; I had no preconceived ideas; I had given them up; I was willing to learn. I had, one might say, turned a mental somersault, so that what may appear upside down to some hon. members looks straight up to me.
I believe that Major Douglas is one of the greatest and most original thinkers of all time. It is said that he is not an economist and he cannot know anything about economics. The greatest astronomer who ever lived believed that the sun went around the earth; he never could accept the theory that the earth went around the sun. In spite of that he is justly considered the greatest astronomer of all time, because he spent his life in taking most accurate measurements of the movements of the stars, and it was through the facts that he made available that Newton was able to reduce the study of the whole solar system to an exact science and to prove mathematically, through his discovery of gravitation, that the earth goes around the sun. It is true that Douglas was not a professional economist; he was an engineer and a thinker. Newton was not an astronomer; he was a philosopher, and so is Douglas. I say that Douglas is the Newton of economics, because, as Newton discovered or established the proof that the earth goes around the sun, Douglas has provided the proof that no longer does our economic system revolve around production but that it revolves around consumption, and that if we look after consumption, production will look after itself, but the reverse process will not work, because modern science and modern productive methods have made that impossible. The replacement of labour by machine has upset the balance, so we say that if we look after consumption1, production will look after itself. That is all we wish to do.
We have been called "red." I know from my own experience that the most bitter opponents we have are the communists. We have nothing whatever to do with communism ' we wish to avoid either extreme : we have no use for fascism and no use for communism. We say that we, the people, should be able to consume to the limits of our desires or of our abilities to produce, whichever comes first; that is all.

Democracy, by Major Douglas, a copy of which is in the parliamentary library. He has this to say:
The complaint which is levelled at the banks is generally that they pay too large a dividend. Now curiously enough, in my opinion, almost the only thing which is not open to destructive criticism about the banks is their dividend. Their dividend goes to shareholders and is purchasing power, but their enormous concealed profits ... do not provide purchasing power for anyone, and merely aggrandize banks as banks. But the essential point in the position of banks, which is so hard to explain, and which is grasped by so very few people, is that their true assets are not represented by anything actual at all, but are represented by the difference between a society functioning under centralized and restricted credit and a free society unfettered by financial restrictions.
We have it from the biggest banker in the British Empire that banks control the policies of the governments and hold in the hollow of their hands the destinies of the people. I do not think anyone in this chamber could successfully deny that statement. We say that that control, that monopoly of credit and money-and without money no one can live, so that, as Mr. McKenna says, those who control money control the lives and hold the destinies of the people in their hands-should be restored to the government in trust for the people.
