Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): The resolution now under discussion, as indicated by many of the addresses to which we have listened, is that kind of omnibus resolution which may mean anything. The fact that it may mean anything is evidenced by the manner in which several hon. members, admittedly differing with the mover of the resolution and his exposition of the meaning of it, nevertheless found in it a means of conveying to the house their particular ideas with respect to what is sometimes, rather loosely I fear, called monetary reform; and they were able therefore to

Purchasing Power-Mr. Dunning
indicate their support of the resolution while disagreeing profoundly with the mover of it in his statement of the case in favour of it. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), for instance, in an address which was admirable so long as he discussed economics prior to embarking upon the political portion of his speech, demolished completely all of the arguments of the mover of the resolution; but he concluded his speech by saying that he would support the resolution because he favoured a mild, small, cautious dose of inflation. The hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) intimated that they would support the resolution because they frankly believe in currency and credit inflation.
I am opposed to the resolution because I believe that nothing could do Canada more harm in this year 1937 than for the idea to go abroad that this House of Commons favoured currency and credit inflation. Certainly any one reading the speeches delivered to-day in favour of the resolution could reach no other conclusion than that in varying degrees the speakers favoured some amount of inflation. Some describe it as scientific inflation, others as controlled inflation; but always inflation was the end of the road reached by various speakers. Various speakers of the social credit group recognize frankly the evils of inflation, recognize indeed that their proposals involve inflation, and they have various suggestions, just as Major Douglas has, to prevent the human suffering which inflation invariably produces.
Briefly put, the social philosophy, as explained by its advocates, proposes arbitrarily to control the price level, by that means avoiding if possible the evils which admittedly flow from uncontrolled inflation. But inasmuch as an increased price level is the major benefit claimed for inflation, I find it difficult to see how it is possible to get the benefits of an increased price level while by arbitrary means preventing the price level from rising.
I am sorry I cannot agree with the hon. member for Rosthem that Canada should copy German financial and economic methods at present in force. Methods which are tolerated by a people willing to make the sacrifice of lowering their standard of living to the irreducible minimum in order to increase their military strength surely should not be advocated by those who profess to
desire an improved standard of living in Canada. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) expressed my views when he said in concluding his remarks:
You cannot in this world get something for nothing without taking that something away from somebody else.
I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar used words carrying almost a similar meaning. More and more as I have listened last session and this, to speeches by those who call themselves monetary reformers, I see the tendency to preach the doctrine that thrift is unsound, that the man who saves a portion of the proceeds of his labour to-day so that he may have the use of it when he can no longer work is somehow an enemy of society. The whole philosophy of social credit is opposed to thrift; it expresses itself frankly as opposed to life insurance, for instance. To me, it seems that, followed to its logical conclusion, this whole argument leads to the point where nobody need work- the state will provide; nobody need save anything-the state will provide. A sort of brain trust bureaucracy by manipulating pieces of paper will plan to give everybody what he needs from birth to death.
In his reference to the international standard of gold backing the hon. member for Rosthern mentioned twenty-five per cent. That is a correct figure except for the qualification that the twenty-five per cent is internationally agreed upon as a minimum. It is correct to say that Canada is not down to the minimum; Canada still has some leeway from the international point of view. From the domestic point of view parliament has entrusted to the Bank of Canada the function of regulating currency and credit in the public interest. Obviously information regarding the day to day discharge of this function cannot be given, but results show clearly the broad line of policy which has been followed by that bank.
I think it may be said with safety that for credit-worthy borrowers, individual, corporate, municipal, provincial and dominion, there prevail to-day in Canada lower interest rates than ever before were known in Canada's history; and I submit that an easy money policy is the best policy for Canada at the present time, however unpopular it may be to those who have money to lend. But, Mr. Speaker, our testing time will come whenever, by means of a too high price level inducing wild speculation in commodities, stocks, et cetera, it becomes desirable in the public in-

Yes, Mr. Speaker. One of the results of the great war and what followed was that tendency, that necessity

Purchasing Power-Mr. Bennett
on the part of practically all countries in the world. Some were slower to come to it than others; all hesitated because of what the facts of history teach with respect to it, and it was only when reasonable unanimity of approach to the problem was secured that the world commenced to rise out of the depression. To-day the relative exchange values of the British pound sterling, the American dollar and the Canadian dollar are marching along steadily. They are not subject to the wild fluctuations in relative values which affected them prior to the commencement of the upturn. I think it is correct to say that the financial statesmanship of the world, during the years from 1930 to 1933 or 1934, was much more exercised with that problem than with all other financial problems put together. It was not until, I would not say a solution was reached, but until reasonable harmony was established that it was possible for that confidence to be created upon which is based the exchange between peoples of their surplus commodities. Indeed, I shall go as far as to say that the adjustment, the management which now exists between the leading currencies of the world was an absolutely necessary preliminary to the revival of international trade; that without it I doubt the possibility of the revival measures which have been taken by various governments of various countries being at all effective.
I have little more to say, Mr. Speaker. All history teaches us the appeal which proposals of this kind have to the ears of men and women who are experiencing great hardship. There never has been in any modern country a time of hardship which did not have as a part of its phenomena a development of so-called monetary reform which always received for a time in all countries very wide support. In some countries the effort was made, with results that are written large on the pages of history, results which drove the common people of those countries further into the mire than they were ever driven by any depression. In other countries, notably the great republic to the south, the agitation for monetary inflation lasted in various forms for a long period of years. It was never successful. I would not use the term " monetary reform " because I do not regard inflation as monetary reform. I regard uncontrolled inflation as the worst kind of monetary reaction. It is destructive.
Moreover, sir, I still believe in the virtue of thrift, I still believe that a man in the full flush of his manhood has not merely the right but the duty to himself and to those who depend upon him to set aside in any manner
which seems good to him a portion of the proceeds of his labour to-day in order that he and those dependent upon him may not later be dependent upon the state. To my mind the strength of the state is the strength of that spirit of independence among the individuals composing the state, and nowhere is that spirit of independence stronger than it- is upon the western plains. Nowhere is it stronger; nowhere is it more pronounced; no people will respond to it more readily. Today they are ground under the heel of climatic conditions unprecedented on this continent.

And of the government. I can only repeat that there is every reason in the world why members who supported the Liberal party at the last election should take the view which has found expression in this house to-day. How could it be otherwise?
What was said from this side of the house during the long years in which we were endeavouring to lay the foundation to which the hon. member to-night referred? What was the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) doing? What was the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) doing? The avowed exponents of the principles of the then opposition cheered loudly and voci-

Purchasing Power-Mr. Bennett
ferously, yes, cheered day after day, as he attacked the financial policies of the then government, and declared what his party would do had they the opportunity.
I shall not content myself by making that statement, but I shall read from the considered and expressed statement of the present Minister of National Defence as it was made in this city on July 5, 1935, just before the last election.
Canada must, Mr. Mackenzie declared, break down tariff barriers; she must even experiment with international barter if necessary. No, he does not declare for free trade; but for "freer" trade, yes.
Incidental to the housing scheme of the present government which Mr. Mackenzie finds so distressingly half-hearted, he recalls his recent visit to Britain. There, he says, a comprehensive housing scheme promises to eliminate all the slums of London and Glasgow in the next five years.
Ask Mr. Mackenzie where the money is coming from and he doesn't even hesitate with his millions. The government has $110,000,000 of gold now worth $118,000,000. On a 25 per cent reserve basis it can issue notes to the extent of $720,000,000 as against the paltry $259,000,000 now in circulation. Use that extra currency to retire public debt, reduce interest to 2J per cent and you will compel money to seek industrial investment.
That was the statement made by one who is now a responsible minister of the crown, one who has made similar statements in this house, as will be shown by Hansard', and the loud and vociferous cheers of those who sat behind him in the house at that time will be recalled by every member, yes, by every member. They cheered the reading of the Macmillan report, just as it was read this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), and the reading of the Canadian Macmillan report, as it was done this afternoon. Then, amid loud and vociferous cheers, those who now are before me and who were in the house in those days declared that what should be done was to take the action as indicated in the excerpt which I have read. Is it any wonder that when financial leaders of the opposition went into their constituencies and made statements they were believed, as was said by the hon. member for Rosthern this afternoon.
I shall not again traverse the speeches of the first minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I shall not traverse what I said last session, or the statements that he made in this house in declaring what the policy of the Liberal party was. I shall not repeat the language used in those speeches which were given the house by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). I shall not do that, because it has already been done. But the

language that was used, the very words that the first minister used on those occasions, were the words which were coined, so far as the resolution is concerned, by that member himself, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.
And with that slogan in their ears the Liberal party went out and sought the support of Canada. I say it lies with no good grace in the Minister of Finance to make the statements he has made here to-night when we remember the stand of the chief financial critic of the opposition of that day. He was constantly at it, with the Macmillan report in his hands, both the English one and the Canadian one, and with the approval of his leader, because many times I have sat over there and have listened to the present Minister of National Defence as he made statements analogous to the one I have just read. Hon. members will find them written on the pages of Hansard. Is it any wonder, therefore, that we find members of the Liberal party seeking support in their constituencies in the terms of the resolution now before the house? Is it any matter of surprise that they should do so, in view of the lead that was then given them? I am rising only to direct attention to that fact and to one other. Faced with the greatest difficulties known to this country, difficulties such as never have been known before-and for the first time I have heard a responsible minister opposite make reference to them; the minister made reference to them to-night in terms of the real facts-faced with conditions as difficult as they could be, or as bad as they could possibly be, the government of the day battled on. But whenever we spoke of the efforts we were endeavouring to make to deal with the situation, night after night we were met with criticism almost the same, in terms of the language used, as that offered by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) yesterday and the hon. member for Rosthern today.
When reference is made to the issue of $35,000,000, I say that certainly 835,000,000 were issued under the terms mentioned by the hon. member for Rosthern. He has correctly stated the circumstances in connection with this issue. At one time the conditions of this country were so serious that those responsible for its administration were fearful of what might happen from day to day. Although there is no denying that there was opposition from many sources in the country, the experiment was made. But it was not continued because the Bank of Canada was thought to be clothed with sufficient authority to cope with any condition that might arise.

The minister has stated to-night that the Bank of Canada was capable of dealing with any situation of that kind which might arise with respect to either currency or credit.
It will be recalled that following the world conference we did propose and carry through this house a measure by which it was provided that currency might be issued with twenty-five per cent metal backing up to $120,000,000. After that it was to be dollar for dollar. However, when the Bank of Canada Act was passed and in operation, there was no limitation placed upon it because in the very nature of things that reserve bank, which it is, was regarded as having sufficient powers to deal with the situation. It was satisfactory to hear the minister say to-night that that was so. It was satisfactory to those of us who laboured against such opposition in those days to hear from him the statement he made with respect to the Bank of Canada, the usefulness of which has been somewhat impaired by the tinkering which has since taken place, but which we can discuss at another time. It is desirable that the house should realize that the situation which confronted this country was one of extreme gravity, calling for prompt and effective measures if we were not to become bankrupt.
Let me say to hon. members who are present in such numbers on the opposite side to the one they then occupied, that no bank in Canada closed its doors during those days, and that no depositor who had funds in a bank wrote a cheque which was not honoured. That could not be said with respect to our great neighbour to the south. Then there was the difficulty which was encountered by the Bank of England and which, as was known to all, had upon this country repercussions. the full extent and effect of which few people have any understanding of at all.

In the days of inflation a single United States cent was capable of purchasing marks sufficient to equal the prewar mortgage debt of the German Empire. When I read that I thought it was a misprint, but I found that it was correct. Professor Kammener points out the reasons why uncontrolled inflation has always led to one end. Inflation has been practised in this country and in other countries, and will probably be practised in the future in still other countries; but for some strange reason, once you start people on the road to inflation there never seems to be an end until bankruptcy and ruin are reached. That is the history of the world.
Canada is now showing signs of recovery. When I think of the revenues of to-day and compare them with what we had to endeavour to get along with in days gone by; when I think of the shrinkage in trade, not only of this country but of the whole world, and how international trade fell to one-third of what it was before the depression; when I think of the conditions under which we had to struggle, I cannot 'but feel, whatever it may have been necessary to do in times of strain and stress and peril, there is, so far as I can observe, no occasion or necessity for any such action at the moment. I trust that the occasion may never again arise in this country. I trust that we may be able to continue the course which we are now following. But when leaders of public thought and opinion induce their party when in opposition to believe that certain things are possible, and that because they are not done by the government certain evil results follow, they cannot when in power blame those who believed that they were listening to sound statements of the party's view when in oppo-

sition. That, I think, is clearly apparent tonight, but the fact that it is apparent is no reason why for a single moment I should do other than vote against this resolution, not only for the reasons that have been' given by the minister and others, but because I have not changed the opinion which I held when responsibility was ours, nor do I think any of my colleagues have changed their opinions. However great may have been the necessity for taking action of an exceptional nature to deal with exceptional conditions, this is neither the time nor the place nor is it desirable to depart from known, sound rules that will enable us, I trust, not only to continue to revive the fortunes of this country but to make them even greater than they have ever been. That, I believe, is the earnest desire of every member of the house. The fundamental principle is that we must have soundness at least in finance. Many improvements have been and are being made from time to time throughout the world, and we in common with other nations are improving our views and our technique in the general administration of these problems, but we are not departing, I trust, from a rule which is salutary and sound, and which is fundamental to the peaceful and orderly development of our resources and the revival and improvement of our economic conditions.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to close this debate I feel moved to make one observation. I am the more persuaded that the fundamental principles underlying this resolution are sound by reason of the apparently deliberate attempt by those who have spoken against the resolution to distort it. I believe before I get through I shall be able to show that those who have opposed this resolution have consistently distorted it. As one simple illustration, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has just been talking of "uncontrolled inflation." There has not been one member of this house or, so far as I know, anybody in this dominion who has advocated for one single minute uncontrolled inflation. I said the other night time and again that we do not advocate inflation at all. It is easy enough to laugh at matters that we know little about. The word inflation has two meanings: first, a rise in price of goods or a fall in the purchasing power of the dollar or other monetary unit; second-the meaning which the banking fraternity are endeavouring to impress upon the people, and which they have even succeeded in bringing into the dictionaries-that inflation means any kind of money whatsoever which the bankers

Purchasing Power-Mr. Blackmore
do not themselves make. No one, I repeat, is advocating uncontrolled inflation, nor is anyone from this side of the house advocating inflation at all. I have enjoyed this discussion tremendously, but it is altogether too bad that the intelligent minds of this house could not have concentrated their attention on realities instead of on a great many foolish distortions.
Let me proceed now to take up some of
them.	In my remarks to-night I think I shall hardly do more than simply point out some of the silly things that have been said. In the first place the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), who is rapidly gaining in this house a reputation for extravagant and radical remarks, made several statements the other night. Some of them I shall not deal with at all because they are beneath contempt. But take that remark when he said, "What will be purchasing power in that island? It will be production." Well, everyone in his senses agrees that production is purchasing power; everyone knows that. I pointed that out time and again. But the trouble is. if I raise a steer out on the Alberta range, and a man down in Toronto or some other eastern city manufactures shoes, while the steer should be purchasing power for the shoes, and the shoes purchasing power for the steer, nevertheless under the highly complex organization of society to-day, unless there is money between the two, there will never be any means whereby the steer can be purchasing power for the shoes. It is precisely as the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hay-hurst) pointed out the other night. He told the story of an island which had languished because it could not get shark's teeth. Did that island languish because there was not plenty of production on that island? Of course not. It was because there was no medium of exchange on the island. I shall deal with that further as I go along.
Let me say to the hon. member for Huron North, if production is purchasing power, why,
then,	cannot production be used as purchasing power-the coal, for example, of which we have an unlimited quantity in Alberta, and our wheat, our meat, wool, butter and all the other commodities that we produce? Why cannot we use these as purchasing power? Simply because we have at the present time no means whereby we can equitably market these goods without a medium of exchange which we call money. We should be able to buy shoes with this production, this purchasing power, but we cannot do so, and the reason is that our monetary system is not functioning as it should.
Here is another point. The hon. member for Huron North asks: "Why cannot you buy a Royalite well?" Why cannot the government buy a Royalite well when the Bank of England, simply by writing an order on itself, can buy gold and get the gold for nothing? Some people will laugh at that statement, but it is strictly true. For if the Bank of England writes a cheque upon itself for gold, and the man who presents that cheque gets Bank of England bills which cost the Bank of England nothing to print, where has the Bank of England paid anything for the gold? This idea has been gone over time and again, but I shall go over it a little more: This is a statement of the assistant under secretary of the British treasury:
I agree with Major Douglas that banks create money and that trade depression arises from faults of the banking system in discharge of that vital function.
The Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, exChancellor of the Exchequer and chairman of the Midland bank, said:
The amount of money in existence varies only with the action of the banks in increasing or diminishing deposits. They who control the credit of the nation, direct the policy of governments, and hold in the hollow of their hands the destiny of the people.
That should be clear enough. Why all the sidestepping? Why the silly distorting in such a childish manner? The issue is straightforward. Either that man knows what he is talking about, or he does not. If he does, then it is time we sat up and paid close attention to it. If he does not, then it is time we proved it. Major Douglas, in his Monopoly of Credit, has made this statement at page 15:
It may be noted in passing, that this is the same thing as saying that a bank acquires securities for nothing, in the same way that a central bank, such as the Bank of England, may be said to acquire gold for nothing. In each case, of course, the institution concerned writes a draft upon itself for the sum involved, and the general public honours the draft by being willing to provide goods and services in exchange for it.
Those words are straightforward and clear and the meaning is beyond question.
Again, the hon. member for Huron North sneered about the prosperity certificates which Alberta attempted to use. I should like to know why hon. members have dragged Alberta into this debate, which is a purely dominion one.

speechtext:
I cannot remember any time having said that, everything I did not agree with was silly. The hon, member for Huron North made this remark, " Give us the way. We want to know how to do it." Suppose I showed him that an automobile would work, that the automobile was a reality, that the fact was testified to by a hundred pepole; the hon. member, I suppose, would be unwilling to take the automobile unless I could show him exactly how to make it. An hon. member has asked me why I use the word " silly." If that is not evidence enough, perhaps he will get some more as we go on. Certain it is that the men who have worked this proposal out have devised currency commissions and a great number of mechanisms as a result of which it can be put into effect. The trouble is that the majority of these people who are having so much to say about it have never in their lives read a book on economics, and consequently know nothing about it, Another statement, made by the hon. member for Huron North is, "You cannot increase the purchasing power of one group without taking it away from some other." When money was issued by the dominion government and was given out to certain people, did it take anything away from anybody? Of course it did not. A little thought will show that that is egregiously silly. The hon. member will soon find out why the word "silly" was used.
Of course, production is the basis of money, and where goods and services are, money ought to be, because money merely represents goods and services. The hon. member blames Alberta because of the effort she is making to establish a system which properly should be created by a sovereign country. We out in Alberta fully recognized that we should be

facing grave difficulties if we undertook to put social credit into effect in that province, for the simple reason that we had not the power to legislate in regard to legal tender. I say we knew that. But we knew also, from the rate at which intelligence and understanding of this matter were developing over the dominion, that Canada would probably go down to complete ruin before anything was ever done, unless we started to do it. It is an interesting fact that the hon. member for Huron North was busying himself most industriously all through the Alberta campaign writing endless articles to show that it could not be done. Since Mr. Aberhart has been mentioned, I may say that he said, " It cannot be done inside eighteen months." He has been in office only sixteen months, and the hon. member is now trying to force Mr. Aberhart to go a little faster, notwithstanding the fact that in that time we have had two terrible crop failures, the worst failures in the history of the land. All that social credit is is a proposal for distributing goods you already have. We know perfectly well that when you are not producing the goods you cannot distribute them. But the situation we found ourselves faced with was that we could produce goods in limitless abundance but we could not distribute them, and we are getting no assistance. And that sounds perfectly right, nothing at all to laugh about.
In addition, throughout our efforts w.e have had an apparently secret but determined influence exerted against us, in connection with the use of the prosperity certificates, and in preparations to block the use of Alberta credit. Even with regard to the signing of the covenants and getting ready for the voluntary introduction of social credit we have had the same opposition to contend with. Talk about giving a country the right to govern itself! Talk about there being no financial influence over countries and governments! It is terrible.
I turn now to deal with one or two matters that came up the other day in debate. The hon. member for York South and I had, quite good-naturedly, a little disagreement, which I think I had better spend a minute or two to clear up. As appears in Hansard, at page 131, column 1, a little passage occurred between the two of us. I am afraid that unless we clear this matter up there will be doubt in the minds of those who read it later on as to which of us was right or whether we were both wrong.

I will not use it any further; I have several others just as good. To continue the quotation:
. . . the producing and consuming power of that island, the exchanges, as Sir Norman Angell says. It will take a good deal of laughing to explain that away.
Mr. Dunning:	Sir Norman Angell did not
say that.
I did not at that moment wish to contradict the Minister of Finance, but I did think it would probably be a good thing for this house to nave that point cleared up, and therefore I have brought into the chamber on this occasion the pamphlet from which we were quoting, Your Money-Plain Facts in Plain Words by Sir Norman Angell. I believe it would be in the interests of certain hon. members to hear certain passages that appear in that book. I would quote the passage at the top of page 20 which closes the story of the sailor who issued the orders. These are the author's words:
Everybody forgets about it-
That is gold.
Everybody forgets about it since the paper is accepted without question. The gold might have been a bit of gilded lead for all the islanders knew. But it did the trick, and the sailor was wise enough not to "inflate" his currency.
That deals with the first part of it. Now may I turn to page 13 at the bottom of column 2. I fancy that the orthodox financial
people in this house will be astonished to learn their great hero, Sir Norman Angell has this to say on the subject:
Now, it would make no difference to the value of Law's money that it should be "backed" by the resources of the Mississippi valley, or to the French revolutionary money that it should be a mortgage upon the national possessions-
Mark the words:
-if the money were issued ill too great a quantity in relation to the exchange of goods to be effected. Both of the moneys just mentioned became utterly worthless-
These are two of the moneys to which the Minister of Finance referred in such eloquent indignation. Notice what Sir Norman Angell says about them:
Both of the moneys just mentioned became utterly worthless, although all the resources of France and the French empire did "stand back of" them.
If the quantity had been limited it would not have mattered in the least that nothing stood behind them in the material sense.
This must be hard on the hon. gentlemen who contend that there must be a backing.
So long as they were legal currency, and their quantity was limited, their value would have been maintained.
You have noticed, Mr. Speaker, how consistently hon. members who oppose this resolution have tried to bring in uncontrolled inflation. We propose nothing of the kind. Let me continue the quotation:
What wrecked them was their excessive quantity. If the effect of putting material wealth "behind" money is to limit the quantity, to cause it to bear some quantitative relation to goods, the device, of course, serves the purpose of limitation. But it is the limitation of quantity which constitutes the guarantee of its value. Ricardo saw this quite clearly when he wrote:
" There is no point more important in issuing paper money than to be fully impressed with the effects that follow from the principle of limitation of quantity. It is not necessary that paper should be payable in specie to secure its value; it is only necessary that its quantity should be regulated."
Now this truth, that the value of money depends in the last analysis, not upon the material of which it is made, or upon being "backed ' by this or that commodity, but upon its quantity, opens up great possibilities for man.
What we are contending now is that this country should begin to use the possibilities which are open to us.
He is not necessarily in this vital question or money the slave of a circumstance outside his control like the discovery or the failure to make adequate discovery of gold. He can control his money, make it his servant instead ot his master, if he can learn the trick, the technique.
174	COMMONS
Purchasing Power-Mr. Blackmore
There are several other interesting points which I could touch upon, but I suggest that hon. members read the account given in this book of what was done on another island the island of Uap of the Carolines. An interesting story is told showing that the islanders used large stones as money.
I turn now to the comments of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who referred to the cause of inflation. I contended time and again, in the quotations I gave the other night, that when you issue money you must be sure that you have plenty of goods; but when you have plenty of goods you can have plenty of money. That point was entirely ignored by the Minister of Labour. I will ask him this question: Would you give $200,000,000 as bonuses to widows if you had it given to you as a free gift from some great financier like Ford? I think anyone would answer, yes, surely. Well, if you can give $200,000,000 as bonuses to widows would it cause inflation? No, of course not, because we know that there are enough goods and services in the dominion to absorb $200,000,000. Would you consider tourist traffic money sound? Yes, surely. Would you consider public works money sound? Yes, it is sound. The Minister of Labour said it was sound; he saw no way in which it would serve as a real solution, though nevertheless it was sound. Therefore I say it would not cause inflation.
Mr. Aberhart and the question of dividends have been dragged into this discussion. I do not see the reason for all this restless haste on the part of some hon. members. If they will wait long enough we will bring in dividends. They do not need to run ahead of us, for I fancy that we are now going as fast as they can keep up with us. They can leave the matter entirely to us.
Not more than two or three years ago men were talking about over-production; we had more goods then than we knew what to do with. To-day in Alberta you can go into the yards of many manufacturers and find stacks of goods that will never be sold. Why should there not be money to move these goods? We already have production; why not have the money that represents that production?
I am going to read a word or two more about inflation. That seems to be the thing people are determined to talk about, and so I shall quote a passage which I read yesterday and which apparently has not been noticed. It appears in World Finance Since 1914, by Paul Einzig, published in 1935.

I quote from page 17:
The more advanced definitions of inflation duly allow for any change in the volume of real wealth. Thus if the volume of currency and credit increases, and the production of real wealth increases in the same proportion, then there is no reason why the expansion of currency and credit should produce an inflationary effect, even if it affects the spending power of the community. It is only if the increase of currency and credit is in excess of the additional production of real wealth that it is defined as being of inflationary character.
The whole contention of the social credit advocates is that we are now living in an age of abundance, and what we have not at present we can produce; consequently the danger of inflation which might have prevailed in the past is now in large measure removed because of our tremendous ability to produce goods.
This is another passage which appeared in the Midland Bank Review for July and August, 1935, at page 3:
In the circumstances now existing there need be no fear that an expansion of note circulation, even if it demands an increase in the fiduciary issue, is inflationary. In this country inflation, if it comes at all, comes not through the note issue, but through bank deposits which are the governing portion of the money supply.
Let m,e break in here, Mr. Speaker, to point this out:	This is the danger which
we face. It is inflation from bank deposits. We lift our hands in horror in this house at the thought of producing a hundred million dollars of national money, but we would not hesitate at all to allow the banks, for example, to produce four hundred million dollars of bank money. That could not cause inflation at all'. You see how inconsistent this kind of thinking is. Now I continue quoting:
Nor can expansion of the note issue be taken even as secondary evidence of inflation unless commodity prices' show a strong upward movement, gathering momentum and threatening to require strong measures for its arrest. So long as a pound note buys a steady amount of goods and services there can be no inflation even though a larger population and a higher standard of living call for more and more numerous pound notes.
I believe that ought to be sufficient for all those who read with care. It is quite clear.	_
There are certain questions about which I believe we should talk. It is noteworthy that Where money supply falls off production falls off. This has been discovered to a surprising degree in the United States, and they are quite astonished at it. They lost a tremendous amount of their national production because a great deal of their money was withdrawn. The question which naturally

Purchasing Power-Mr. Blackmore
arises in the minds of ail those thinking about this matter is why, by some means or another, the money supply could not have been kept up and thus the production kept up and used to supply the needs of the people suffering in poverty. That is the whole contention, and the chief point to ibe considered. In Canada to-day we have unemployment and suffering, but not because we cannot produce all the things we need. We can produce all the beef, flour, milk and cream, eggs, butter and coal that we require. I do not know how many different commodities there are; there must be scores and scores of them. We can produce them in abundance, more than we can possibly use; yet we allow people right in the presence of these goods to suffer. Only money can distribute these goods, and the problem is to get that money into circulation. The banks cannot circulate it for the simple reason that bankers cannot let out money except as loans. That is where the problem lies.
Now I come to the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). From the way this hon. gentleman spoke it appeared to me that there must be a terrible fear that someone will consume something he has not produced. Well, no one seems to be concerned about the amount consumed by those men who receive huge pensions. No one is worrying at all about that. If we had a multimillionaire in Canada whose property passed on to his children, no one would ever worry because they consumed what they had never produced. But some poor person who is out of employment, and who is unable to get a job no matter where he goes, must not use what he does not produce. Does that sound wonderfully intelligent?
There is another very important point, the concentration of money, which the hon. member also mentioned. We are aware of the concentration of money. What advantage would it be to a community if there were a million dollars in that- community and all that money was in the hands of ten people, while there were thousands who needed the money? If they could not get the money out of the hands of those ten people what should they do, just stand there and starve to death? Why not have new money, as they had before these few men got the million dollars? There is the problem. How can you get the money away from the man in whose hands it is now concentrated? You have no right to confiscate that money or tax it all away. If you borrow it you must pay it back with interest, and go into debt, and then you have to keep their commandments both before and after you borrow it. What are you to do? That is the question. You are at their mercy. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar does not seem to have taken that into account at all.
There is another point that I have noticed particularly in connection with the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group. I have not said anything to them about it as yet, but these people appear to be tremendously worried for fear the social credit people will not be able to tell this house what they believe in. Consequently these gentlemen are bobbing up three or four times every month trying to tell this house what members of the social credit party believe in. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that social credit is completely capable of speaking for itself.
Then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) made some statements which, I think, were probably rather ill considered. He has been extremely good natured and tolerant about this matter; he and I have had a little difference, but I feel very kindly towards hon. members opposite even though I did use the word "silly." But if my ears did not deceive me the Minister of Finance made the positive statement that social credit opposes life insurance. I cannot remember ever hearing that social credit opposed life insurance. Certainly no member in this house has said anything about that. Why make a remark of that kind to divert the attention of the people away from the real issue?
Then the Minister of Finance made the remark that our well-being depends upon our national income. The other night I quoted figures from good authorities in the United States, where men have investigated this question with great care, to show that the income of the country depends directly upon the amount of money in circulation in the country, and for every S3 of income, wages, salaries, dividends or anything else, there must be $1 in circulation. If the Minister of Finance and the government are so completely desirous of increasing the national income, it seems to be strongly suggested that they could do so by increasing the money in circulation, which apparently they are not at all disposed to do.
I maintain that national money gradually issued will not cause inflation or, in other words, a rise in prices. No evidence, has been brought forward during the course of this debate to show that this result will follow. In this chamber no one has risen, in connection with any of the issues of money mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosthern, to say that this caused inflation, and

Purchasing Power-Mr. Blackmore
no one can prove that it did. If anyone can do so I shall be a ready listener. If $50,000,000 or $35,000,000 were used with no dangerous results, who is to say that $35,000,000 a month for a number of months necessarily would bring about dangerous results?
In consideration of the matters I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, I believe I am justified in saying once more that whereas it is legal for this country to issue national purchasing power; whereas there is no sufficient and conclusive evidence that the issue of national purchasing power would cause inflation, and whereas the need for new money is very grave in this country, for a great number of reasons, I do not hesitate to ask the members of this house to support this resolution. But before taking my seat there is one further point to which I should like to direct the attention of the house, another slight discrepancy in the remarks of the Minister of Finance. The hon. gentleman said that if this house adopted this resolution it would commit itself to the idea of inflation.
